clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive hypomyelinating leukodystrophy caused by variants in FAM126A, which encodes the protein hyccin
The combination of congenital or early-infantile cataract with a hypomyelinating leukodystrophy is the diagnostic signature and should prompt FAM126A testing
Children typically develop cataract in the first months of life, followed by delayed motor milestones, progressive spasticity, cerebellar ataxia and a peripheral neuropathy
The peripheral neuropathy is an important feature that distinguishes this disorder from many other hypomyelinating leukodystrophies confined to the central nervous system
MRI shows diffuse hypomyelination together with additional periventricular white matter T2 hyperintensity that extends beyond the background hypomyelination
Cognition is often relatively preserved compared with the degree of motor disability, at least earlier in the course

Diagnosis rests on the cataract-plus-leukodystrophy phenotype with neuropathy, supported by MRI and confirmed by FAM126A sequencing; management is supportive with cataract surgery, physiotherapy and rehabilitation
reference.pathophysiology: Hypomyelination with congenital cataract is caused by biallelic variants in FAM126A, which encodes hyccin, a membrane-associated protein that forms part of a complex regulating phosphatidylinositol-4-phosphate synthesis at the plasma membrane. This lipid signalling is important for the function of myelinating cells and the lens. Loss of hyccin impairs central myelination by oligodendrocytes and peripheral myelination by Schwann cells, producing a combined central hypomyelination and peripheral neuropathy, while disturbed lens homeostasis leads to the characteristic early cataract.
additionalDifferentials: Other hypomyelinating leukodystrophies (Pelizaeus-Merzbacher and Pelizaeus-Merzbacher-like disease)
Congenital cataract with metabolic disease (galactosaemia, peroxisomal and Lowe syndrome)
Cockayne syndrome and other disorders combining cataract with leukoencephalopathy
Cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis (juvenile cataract with neurological decline)
additionalInvestigations: Ophthalmological assessment to confirm and characterise the cataract
Brain MRI to demonstrate hypomyelination with additional periventricular white matter signal change
Nerve conduction studies to document the associated peripheral neuropathy
FAM126A sequencing, with hypomyelinating leukodystrophy panel or exome if negative
Metabolic screen to exclude treatable causes of infantile cataract
Developmental and physiotherapy assessment to guide rehabilitation
redFlags: Untreated dense cataract threatening irreversible amblyopia in infancy
Rapid neurological regression prompting reassessment for an alternative diagnosis
Dysphagia with aspiration as bulbar involvement progresses
Loss of ambulation from combined spasticity and neuropathy
reference.prognosis: The disorder is progressive but often relatively slow, with gradually worsening spasticity, ataxia and neuropathy over childhood; many children lose independent walking in later childhood or adolescence, though cognition may be comparatively spared. Prognosis varies with the specific variants and the degree of peripheral nerve involvement.
pitfalls: Treating the cataract in isolation without recognising the associated leukodystrophy and neuropathy
Overlooking the peripheral neuropathy, a key clue separating this from other hypomyelinating disorders
Not obtaining MRI to identify the additional periventricular white matter change
Assuming an isolated congenital cataract syndrome and missing FAM126A genetics
Failing to provide autosomal recessive genetic counselling
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
